has to do with one of the ways DDOS protection works.

DDOS is often described as a "war of money" - that is, the attacker tries to pay for/acquire illictly though expensive skills enough infrastructure to send you more (pointless) requests than your servers can handle, and the website/service tries to pay for enough infrastructure to be able to handle all those requests in addition to normal intended usage.

Good DDOS protection is about providing ways to handle a larger number of requests without increasing costs proportionately.

Some of this 'good DDOS protection' must be done in-house, others can be done by DDOS protection services like cloudflare. One such 'good DDOS protection' method is taking advantage of the economy of scale DDOS protection services have.

The DDOS protection provider is a big business which works tirelessly to get cheap bandwidth.

Many DDOS attackers are amateurs using powerful but unsophisticated tools that make use of botnets or cloud services to orchestrate lots of requests.

Because additional bandwidth has higher costs to them than the cloud service provider, in a war of bandwidth with the cloud service provider (though not with servers hosted elsewhere), the attacker will lose.

The way to make this war happen is to make the attacker spend the majority of bandwidth (incoming and outgoing) on an intermediary page many times they visit the site.

The downside of this is that it increases bandwidth costs for ordinary users. The upside is that those ordinary users will still get to be users in the first place, and still get to see the site they came to view.

Yeah, this blocks certain classes of DDOS, not all. For example this works well against attackers trying to imitate normal traffic as closely as possible to make filtering, source address blacklisting, etc, harder.

It won't a block a SYN flood, but there are other things you do for that, (RST, etc), which wouldn't work against the "imitate normal traffic" DDOS.

BotNets are a relatively mature economy and there are many illicit operations competing for use of them (e.g. identity theft and other fraud), so they can get expensive. The people paying for botnets are either people who pay a DDOS service that controls or rents a botnet, or the script kiddies mentioned above who are usually using rented botnets vs. using a script to develop a botnet.

The reason people pay is because it's less risky and less work: there are plenty of people willing to risk prison for money (botnet owners), less so for DDOS attacking their enemies (botnet renters).

In regard to personally developing your own botnet, it takes a lot of time from someone with a lot of skill (usually more than one person) to start and scale up a botnet to the point you could challenge a DDOS protection provider like CloudFlare, and then use it strictly for DDOS ignoring the vast amounts you could be making by renting it out.

In a way though, you are still getting them at below market cost, and you're right that when this does happen it is a hard class of attackers to counter.

The idea is obviously inspired as an alternative to the now-dismissed limits based on SCP and CCPs, and it goes like this: every user has a web of trust, on which other users go up/down the chain based on the upvoats/downvoats they receive by said user. Trust manifests in the form of a higher weight given to contributions and up/downvoats from the users.

EXAMPLE: assume that the weight is given by the ratio between up/downvoats given to total up/downvoats given. User A has given 20 upvoats totally, 10 of which to contributions from user B. B weights +50% for A. User B has given 100 upvoats, 10 of which to user C. C weights +10% for B. By network effect, C weights +5% for A. User B writes a post that has 23 total raw score, including an upvoat from C. User A sees the post with 23.55 total score.

Benefits of this mechanism:

  • it encourages contributions (only way to move up/down in the web of trust);
  • it reduces the impact of vote-only sock puppet accounts;
  • it reduces the impact of brigading over the longer term.

Issues:

  • most important, computational/storage cost; even though the web of trust is typically rather sparse, there's still the potential for 10^12 combinations needed to store it for 1M users;
  • brigading effect still visible to newcomers/logged-out users; this might require a ‘global’ web of trust built from the individual users'.

Non-issue:

  • circlejerking shouldn't be more of an issue than it is now, and its effects will still be limited to the circlejerkers.

This is obviously just a quick draft, but I'm throwing it here because I'm sure Voat collectively can improve it faster than I can on my own.

EDIT #1: here's a mathematical formulation of the proposal, hoping it will make things clearer.

Call V the matrix where V(i,j) is the (normalized) number of ups/downs user i has given to user j (i is the row index, j is the column index). Call W the matrix where W(i, j) is the weight user i gives to contributions by user j.

V(i,j) is known, and has 0 on the diagonal. The diagonal elements of W(i,j) are 1, and the off-diagonal elements are the unknown weights we want to want to compute.

The weights should satisfy the relation that W(i,j) = sum W(i,k)*V(k,j) (i.e. the sum of the opinions of user j by all users k, corrected by the weight the opinion of user k has for user i). The right-hand side is just W.V, but keep in mind this only holds for the off-diagonal elements. The definition of W is thus the solution of the fixed-point equation

W = W.V + (I - diag(W.V))

where I is the identity matrix of the correct rank and diag() is a function that returns the matrix diagonal (in practice, what the expression in parenthesis is doing is to replace the diagonal of W.V with the diagonal of the identity matrix, to give 1). I'm currently looking for a simpler expression that wouldn't require sophisticated algebra packages to quickly find a solution.
